metadata.title: Proceedings of 1st International Workshop on Renewable Energies. Advances, Challenges and Global Perspectives
metadata.description:
The 1st International Workshop on Renewable Energies: Advances, Challenges, and
Global Perspectives, organized by the RIBIERSE-CYTED network, provided an
academic forum for discussion and exchange focused on analyzing the main scientific,
technological, and social advances related to the transition to sustainable energy
systems. The RIBIERSE-CYTED network held this workshop virtually on July 1 and
2, 2026, bringing together researchers, energy sector professionals, institutional
representatives, and stakeholders interested in the development, integration, and
consolidation of renewable energies in local, regional, and global contexts.

The contributions presented in the proceedings book highlight the diverse approaches
in the field of renewable energy. The included papers cover a range of topics, including
the operation and maintenance of renewable energy plants, the application of artificial
intelligence and computational tools for energy optimization, the design of microgrids,
and energy communities supported by renewable technologies and storage.
Additionally, they address the social, regulatory, and legislative factors that have
influenced the implementation of cleaner, more resilient, and equitable energy models.
This volume brings together contributions that emphasize the necessity of integrating
scientific knowledge, technological innovation, industrial experience, and social
perspectives to address the contemporary challenges of decarbonization, energy
efficiency, and supply security. Moreover, the compiled research identifies emerging
trends, explores opportunities for international collaboration, and outlines work to
strengthen renewable energy in the context of sustainable development.

The editors express their gratitude to the authors, speakers, participants, and
collaborating entities that made this first international workshop possible. It is hoped
that these proceedings will help disseminate knowledge, strengthen academic and
professional networks, and promote innovative solutions for a just, efficient, and
globally relevant energy transition.

metadata.title: Bayesian Diagnostic Insights: A Software Tool for Applying Bayes' Theorem in Medical Diagnostics
metadata.description: This software tool is a specialized program developed in Wolfram Language for the parametric estimation, visualization, and comparison of Bayesian diagnostic measures and their uncertainty. The program utilizes Bayes' theorem to compute the posterior probabilities for disease and absence of the disease, as well as the diagnostic threshold-derived positive and negative predictive values. It uses advanced uncertainty propagation methods to quantify their standard sampling, measurement, and combined uncertainty using normal, lognormal, and gamma distributions. The tool enhances the estimation process and facilitates the comparison of these Bayesian diagnostic measures, which are critical for medical practice. Furthermore, it provides a robust framework for analyzing uncertainty, thereby aiding in the understanding and applying of probabilistic methods in medical diagnostics.
metadata.notes: Bayesian Diagnostic Insights can be run on Wolfram Player® or Wolfram Mathematica®

metadata.title: Sociology of the Digital Divide: Examining Social Inequality in Technology Access and Digital Literacy
metadata.description:
Abstract 

The "digital divide"—the gap between those with access to modern information and communication technologies (ICT) and those without—remains a critical sociological concern in the 21st century. This article explores the multidimensional nature of this divide, moving beyond mere physical access to examine disparities in digital literacy, utility, and socioeconomic outcomes. By applying established sociological theories, including Pierre Bourdieu's concepts of capital and Manuel Castells' theories on the network society, this paper analyzes how technology exacerbates existing inequalities based on race, class, and geography. We argue that digital exclusion is not an isolated phenomenon but a reproduction of systemic societal stratification, requiring a transition from viewing this as a technological hurdle to understanding it as a sociological crisis of agency and citizenship. This expanded study further investigates how emerging technologies like AI and automated systems further entrench these divides, necessitating a radical rethinking of digital rights as basic human rights.

Keywords: Digital Divide, Social Inequality, Digital Literacy, Sociology of Technology, Social Capital, Datafication, Network Society, Digital Agency

1. Introduction: The Evolution of Digital Disenfranchisement

The digital divide is no longer merely defined by the presence of a computer or an internet connection; it has matured into a multi-layered phenomenon concerning the competence to navigate the digital landscape effectively. In the contemporary "network society," technology functions as a fundamental prerequisite for social participation. Those lacking the skills to leverage digital tools—from applying for government benefits to participating in remote work—face profound social exclusion. This is a transformation of citizenship; as the public sphere migrates to digital architectures, the inability to access or master these tools constitutes a form of "digital disenfranchisement."

We must transition from viewing this as a technological hurdle to understanding it as a sociological crisis of agency. When connectivity becomes the gatekeeper for healthcare, education, and political engagement, the lack of digital access functions as a modern barrier to the fundamental rights of participation in the economic, political, and cultural life of the nation-state. This study examines how digital inclusion is not just about "hardware," but about the structural integration of individuals into the digital economy. As society becomes increasingly "datafied," the divide shifts from a binary state of online/offline to a spectrum of varying degrees of participation, where the quality of one's digital experience is directly proportional to their socioeconomic status.

Furthermore, the "digital-first" policy shift by governments globally has inadvertently created a tier of "invisible citizens." These are individuals who, due to age, disability, or lack of resources, cannot interact with the state through its primary digital interfaces. This exclusion is not just an inconvenience; it is a systematic stripping of the individual's ability to claim their rights, access their pensions, or receive medical information. The sociological implication here is the creation of a "technological underclass" whose lack of digital literacy renders them effectively stateless within their own administrative systems. This underclass is characterized by a "circular exclusion"—where the inability to navigate digital systems prevents access to the resources (like education or employment) that would allow them to acquire the necessary digital skills.

2. Theoretical Framework: Bourdieu and the Network Society

Sociologically, the digital divide is best understood through the lens of Bourdieu’s cultural capital. Digital literacy acts as a form of capital; it is a learned disposition—a "digital habitus"—that allows individuals to extract value from the digital sphere. When educational institutions and labor markets assume digital fluency, they privilege those who have acquired this habitus at home, thereby reinforcing class distinctions under the guise of technological neutrality. This "habitus" involves not just the operational ability to click buttons, but the cognitive flexibility to navigate complex UI/UX, evaluate the credibility of information, and manage digital identity.

Furthermore, the social capital generated through digital networks is unevenly distributed. Elite groups use digital tools to solidify their professional networks, whereas marginalized groups may use them for basic consumption, failing to convert digital presence into social mobility. Manuel Castells’ conceptualization of the "network society" reinforces this: those outside the network are not just offline; they are structurally marginalized from the flows of power, information, and capital. The digital sphere, rather than acting as a democratizing "great equalizer," often functions as a mirror reflecting and amplifying existing social hierarchies. In this framework, the digital divide is not merely a gap in technology, but a mechanism of social closure that prevents the upward mobility of those lacking the requisite digital dispositions.

Expanding on this, we must consider the concept of "symbolic violence" in the digital age. When digital platforms impose rigid, Western-centric, and youth-oriented design standards, they implicitly signal that those who struggle to adapt are "outdated" or "unproductive." This narrative of technological inferiority serves to justify the exclusion of the poor and elderly. The digital habitus is therefore not neutral; it is a manifestation of institutional power that favors the dominant classes who already possess the requisite linguistic and cultural codes to thrive in digital environments. This dominance is maintained through the normalization of "fast-paced" digital consumption, which inherently favors those with the leisure time and cognitive resources to constantly adapt to new platform updates and interfaces.

3. Table 1: Dimensions of the Digital Divide

Level Focus Sociological Impact
First-Level Physical Access Infrastructure inequality & spatial segregation
Second-Level Digital Literacy Competence, usage gap, and social habitus
Third-Level Outcome Gap Tangible socioeconomic benefits and mobility
Fourth-Level Datafication Algorithmic bias and control over digital identity
Fifth-Level Agency Loss of political participation and digital citizenship

4. Case Study 1: Education in Rural India

During the COVID-19 pandemic, the shift to online education acted as a catalyst for educational stratification in India. Students in urban centers with high-speed fiber optics were able to maintain continuity, while rural students, lacking reliable electricity and devices, faced a complete cessation of learning. The "rural penalty" here is not just about signal; it is about the institutional failure to provide the infrastructure necessary for equitable access, leading to permanent regression in literacy rates. Sociologically, this creates a "lost generation" in rural areas, where the lack of digital pedagogical tools forces them out of competitive streams, further concentrating professional opportunities in urban, tech-literate populations.

The long-term consequence is the solidification of rural poverty, as these children enter the workforce at a structural disadvantage. Moreover, the lack of digital pedagogical resources reinforces traditional patriarchal norms in households where mobile devices are often prioritized for male family members, further widening gender gaps in educational attainment within rural settings. This gendered divide is a crucial indicator of how technology, in the absence of egalitarian policies, mirrors and deepens existing domestic power structures. The "lost generation" is not merely a group of students who missed lessons; it is a cohort that has been structurally excluded from the new "networked" version of the Indian economy, pre-emptively capping their social mobility. This exclusion effectively traps rural families in low-value agricultural or manual labor, as their children are unable to participate in the growing service and technology-driven sectors that now mandate digital certification.

5. Digital Literacy Rates by Socioeconomic Status

Table 2:Digital Literacy Rates by Socioeconomic Status

Status Basic Literacy Advanced Digital Literacy Utility in Economic Advancement
High-Income 98% 85% High
Middle-Income 92% 45% Moderate
Low-Income 75% 15% Negligible
Precariat Class 60% 5% Non-existent

6. Case Study 2: The Gig Economy in Brazil

Platform-based work promised autonomy, but the digital divide in Brazil reveals a harsher reality. Only workers with high digital fluency—those who understand how to optimize search algorithms, manage digital ratings, and navigate complex interfaces—can successfully "game" the system to maximize earnings. Conversely, those with limited literacy are trapped in a cycle of high-risk, low-wage tasks, effectively recreating traditional class exploitation within a digital framework. This reveals a new form of "digital labor exploitation," where the platform assumes the role of a taskmaster that uses technical opacity to obscure the mechanics of wealth extraction.

This is compounded by the "algorithmic management" of workers, where decisions regarding work allocation are made by opaque systems that favor those who can "perform" for the algorithm. The lack of legal protections for these workers is not accidental; it is a structural byproduct of a system that views digital labor as infinitely replaceable and technically managed, rather than as a human service. The gig economy in Brazil, while providing entry-level access to the labor market, functions primarily as a digital panopticon where worker productivity is surveilled and penalized with minimal human recourse. The divide here is not just one of access, but of the capability to negotiate one's own labor conditions within a platform architecture that is designed to minimize labor costs at the expense of worker stability. This creates a "digital reserve army of labor," where platforms can easily switch to cheaper, more desperate workers at the touch of a button, ensuring that wages remain perpetually low despite the high intensity of work demanded by the app.

7. Gender Disparities in ICT Usage

Table 3: Gender Disparities in ICT Usage

Region Male Usage Female Usage Sociological Context
Developed Nations 95% 94% Near parity, focus shifts to usage depth
Developing Nations 62% 48% Cultural barriers and limited educational access
Urban Clusters 85% 78% Economic empowerment via small business apps
Conflict Zones 40% 20% Security concerns and gendered social norms

8. Case Study 3: Aging Populations in the UK

The "silver surfers" movement faces systemic exclusion due to age-related cognitive hurdles and interface design that prioritizes youth-centric patterns. This is not merely an individual failure to learn; it is a structural exclusion where the "default user" is defined as a younger, tech-savvy individual. When the state migrates pension, health scheduling, and benefit applications to "digital-first" platforms, the elderly are functionally excluded from the social safety net, illustrating how technological design decisions carry deep moral and political consequences.

This exclusion leads to increased loneliness, reduced health outcomes, and a loss of autonomy. The "digitization of the state" requires that the elderly possess a level of digital habitus they were never socialized to acquire, turning their age into a form of social disability in the context of administrative state bureaucracy. This effectively disenfranchises the elderly, stripping them of the ability to self-advocate within systems that are increasingly mediated by invisible algorithms. The sociological tragedy is that these individuals have contributed to the tax base for decades, only to find the services they funded are now accessible only to those who possess the "correct" technological credentials—credentials they were never given the chance to acquire. This creates a state of "digital dependency," where the elderly are forced to rely on younger family members or state caseworkers, eroding the independence that is central to their dignity in their final years.

9. Barriers to Internet Adoption

Table 4: Barriers to Internet Adoption

Barrier Type Prevalence (%) Sociological Driver
Cost 45% Economic Stratification and Poverty
Lack of Interest 25% Cultural alienation from tech-centric society
Lack of Skills 30% Institutional failure in lifelong education
Security Concerns 15% Distrust of institutions and digital surveillance

10. Case Study 4: The Urban-Rural Divide in the USA

Despite various federal initiatives, the "last mile" connectivity problem leaves millions in Appalachian regions without broadband. This geographical isolation limits participation in the remote-work economy, reinforcing the economic decline of these regions. When local economies pivot to digital commerce, those in "dead zones" are effectively disconnected from the national market. Sociologically, this creates "geographic entrapment," where the physical location of a resident prevents participation in the modern digital labor market.

This entrapment exacerbates regional inequalities, often leading to a "brain drain" as young, skilled individuals leave for connected cities, further weakening the local social fabric. The persistence of these "dead zones" is a clear failure of public policy, highlighting how private infrastructure investment models consistently neglect rural populations, thereby codifying regional inequality into the physical geography of the internet. The digital divide, in this context, acts as a self-fulfilling prophecy of decay; the lack of infrastructure prevents the growth of local tech-driven solutions, ensuring that the region remains a "legacy" economy in an era that rewards digital agility. This creates a stark spatial segregation, where the "digital haves" cluster in affluent urban hubs, while the "have-nots" are relegated to the physical margins, further distancing them from the centers of wealth creation.

11. Digital Exclusion and Social Mobility

Table 5: Digital Exclusion and Social Mobility

Access Level Mobility Potential Key Sociological Mechanism
High High Networking and information symmetry
Low Stagnant Limited skill acquisition and social networking
Critical Diminishing Exclusion from essential civic/economic platforms
Absolute Systemic Failure Complete severance from national/global market

12. Case Study 5: Refugee Integration in Germany

Digital access serves as the primary gateway for refugee integration, providing navigation for housing, legal status, and job markets. However, the lack of language-specific digital interfaces or formal training programs creates a "digital border." Refugees who cannot bridge this gap remain isolated from the bureaucratic systems designed to support them, demonstrating how digital exclusion directly affects human rights and civic assimilation.

The "digital border" is as physical as a fence; it creates a zone of exclusion where the migrant cannot access resources promised by the state. This underscores the urgency for inclusive technology design that accounts for linguistic diversity and cultural context. Digital platforms, in this instance, function as a secondary vetting mechanism, where those unable to navigate the digital bureaucracy are effectively deemed "unintegrated" and thus ineligible for state-sponsored social support. The lack of digital access for refugees is not just a logistical hurdle—it is a political barrier that ensures those who are most in need remain the most disconnected, creating a permanent underclass of individuals who are physically present but administratively invisible within the host society.

13. Case Study 6: Racialized Access in South African Townships

Historical infrastructure legacies in South Africa continue to dictate the digital experience. Residents in townships often rely on mobile-only, data-capped internet, while suburban areas enjoy high-speed fiber. This structural disparity limits the quality of information access and the ability to engage in resource-intensive digital activities, reinforcing historical racial economic segregation through modern technological channels.

This is an example of "technological path dependency," where the architecture of the past dictates the limitations of the future. The digital divide in this context is not a new problem but a new iteration of deep-seated racial injustice, where the infrastructure of inequality is maintained via the uneven deployment of modern connectivity. The reliance on mobile-only internet creates a "consumption-only" digital experience, preventing these populations from creating content, managing complex digital assets, or participating in the production side of the digital economy. This is a subtle, systemic exclusion that limits the potential for township residents to leverage the internet as a tool for political or economic liberation, keeping them locked in a cycle of limited digital utility that mirrors the spatial segregation of the Apartheid era.

Conclusion: Policy Implications and the Path Forward

The sociology of the digital divide demonstrates that the problem is deeply embedded in history, class, and policy. Mitigating this divide requires more than hardware distribution; it necessitates a commitment to digital literacy education as a fundamental right and an inclusive approach to technology design. Policies must shift from mere infrastructure deployment to "digital social work"—a holistic approach that recognizes the diverse cultural, economic, and age-related barriers that prevent full integration into the network society.

We propose that universal digital access be reclassified as a basic civic right, similar to water or electricity, with public-private partnerships mandated to prioritize the underserved. Furthermore, education systems must overhaul their curricula to prioritize critical digital literacy, teaching students not just how to use technology, but how to understand the data structures and algorithms that shape their lives. To ignore these sociological dimensions is to allow the digital divide to become a permanent structural feature of the modern world, permanently relegating vast segments of the population to the status of "digital outsiders." Future research must focus on the "fifth-level" divide—the loss of digital agency—and how citizens can reclaim control over the platforms and algorithms that manage their social and civic existence. The path forward requires a radical democratization of the digital infrastructure, ensuring that the "network society" includes everyone, rather than acting as a mechanism for the stratification of the many by the few.

metadata.title: 中医经济学(Traditional Chinese Medicine Economics)
metadata.description:
内容概要:

本书是中医经济学作为一门独立学科的奠基之作。承继前人开拓,本书完成了从“方法论类比”到“本体论革命”、从“政策应用”到“学科体系”、从“哲学思辨”到“科学实证”的三重跃迁,标志着经济学范式的一次深刻变革。

全书二十一章仿照中医“医道”精心构筑,形成“道—体—用—证—诊—治—境”的完整认知闭环:从哲学根基与人性论革命出发,经经济生命体论、气血经络五行等本体构造与运行机理,通过病理分析与诊断辨证,最终归于治疗方略与文明境界。

本书以“经济生命体论”颠覆西方经济学的机械本体论,将经济系统确认为具有自组织、自适应、自我调节能力的生命有机体;以“气血经络五行”重构要素、产业与区域理论,为经济学提供非还原论的整体分析范式。在治理层面,“四诊合参”“八纲辨证”“八法调控”“政策复方”等工具可直接转化为宏观经济决策的操作手册,实现从“逆周期调节”到“辨证管理”、从“挑选赛道”到“调理生态”的方法论跃迁。在危机应对上,“内外合邪”病因学与“扶正祛邪”原则,为防范化解系统性风险提供了超越单一归因的系统方案。本书最终指向中国自主经济学知识体系的构建,为全球治理贡献“阴阳平衡”的东方智慧,使经济学从“修理机器”的技术官僚之学,升华为“调理生命”的治理艺术。

metadata.title: Beyond the Binary of Purity and Pollution: A Sociological Investigation of Contemporary  Neo-Dalit Movements and Digital Resistance in Urban India
metadata.description:
Abstract

This research investigates the profound paradigm shift in contemporary Dalit activism within urban India, moving beyond the traditional Dumontian frameworks of "purity and pollution" which have long dominated the sociological study of caste. Through a critical sociological lens, this paper examines how Neo-Dalit movements leverage digital platforms to construct powerful counter-narratives, mobilize collective identity, and systematically challenge structural inequalities within hyper-modern urban spaces. Utilizing a multi-sited, mixed-methods approach—combining digital ethnography, semi-structured qualitative interviews, and statistical content analysis—this study demonstrates that digital resistance is not merely a supplementary extension of physical protest but a fundamental, generative space for intersectional identity formation that transcends traditional, geographically bound caste hierarchies. Findings suggest that digital platforms facilitate a "virtuous cycle" of political mobilization, effectively connecting hyper-local grievances to expansive, national human rights discourses, thereby altering the traditional topography of power. The paper further critiques how algorithmic governance interacts with legacy social hierarchies, arguing that the digital realm acts simultaneously as an equalizer and a site of renewed structural contestation. By documenting the rise of "digital subalternity," this study provides a comprehensive roadmap for understanding the evolution of caste-based movements in the age of algorithmic capital, offering a new theoretical framework for interpreting the intersection of caste, technology, and urban citizenship.

Keywords: Neo-Dalit, Digital Resistance, Caste, Urban Sociology, Social Media Activism, India, Algorithmic Governance, Subalternity, Digital Public Sphere.

1. Introduction: The Evolving Landscape of Caste

The sociological discourse surrounding caste in India has historically been tethered to the binary of "purity and pollution," a conceptual framework popularized by Louis Dumont in Homo Hierarchicus. In this traditional view, the caste system was perceived as a rigid, ritualized, hierarchical order where social standing was inextricably linked to religious notions of sacred purity and profane impurity. This framework, while historically useful in mapping village-level social structures and the maintenance of traditional hegemony, often obscured the material basis of caste power, the endurance of untouchability in modern spheres, and the agency of those subjected to it.

In the 21st century, the rapid transformation of Indian urban centers—characterized by hyper-modernity, high-speed digital connectivity, and the emergence of a new "urban precariat"—requires a scholarly reappraisal of how caste operates. We are witnessing a transition from caste as a ritual hierarchy to caste as an algorithmic and structural barrier within the urban market economy. The digital age has introduced a new, complex topography of resistance that defies these rigid, traditional categories. Contemporary Neo-Dalit movements in urban India represent a radical departure from established, top-down caste-based organizational patterns, utilizing algorithmic visibility to bypass traditional media gatekeepers that have historically silenced or marginalized Dalit voices.

In the urban context, where anonymity and mobility often clash with lingering caste biases in housing, employment, and social life, the digital realm provides a persistent, accessible site for mobilization. The digital space is not merely a tool; it is an environment where the "politics of dignity" are re-articulated against the backdrop of an indifferent urban state. This paper argues that digital space serves as a "third space"—a hybrid, contested environment where traditional, stigmatized identities are actively deconstructed and new, assertive political subjectivities are forged. By examining the intricate interplay between virtual mobilization and urban structural inequality, we map how digital tools are reconfiguring the politics of dignity.

This investigation asks: How does the transition from physical spaces of exclusion to digital spaces of connection redefine the potential for democratic engagement among the marginalized? We explore how the digital realm allows for the creation of "counterpublics" where Ambedkarite ideologies are translated into viral messaging, effectively challenging the hegemony of traditional media and forcing state accountability in ways that were previously inaccessible to the subaltern. Furthermore, we contend that this shift is not purely emancipatory. As digital platforms become the primary arenas for sociopolitical discourse, they are subjected to algorithmic curation that often replicates, or even amplifies, the historical biases of the offline world. The "digital public sphere" in India is thus a site of intense friction, where the democratizing potential of global connectivity meets the persistence of localized, caste-based gatekeeping.

2. Methodology: Capturing the Digital Subaltern

This research adopts a rigorous triangulation of methods to capture the dynamism and volatility of digital activism across urban Indian centers. The approach acknowledges that digital data is not inherently objective but reflects the socio-technical biases of the platforms themselves.

Table 1:Capturing the Digital Subaltern

Data Source

Method

Sample Size

Objective

Social Media Posts

Content Analysis

5,000 posts

Analyze hashtag trends and discourse patterns

Our methodology relies on the premise that the "digital subaltern" is a data-generating agent. Through deep-canvassing and digital ethnography, we traced the movement of hashtags like #DalitLivesMatter and #DalitHistoryMonth across diverse Indian urban hubs, accounting for regional variations in digital infrastructure and access. This methodological framework allows us to bridge the gap between abstract sociopolitical theory and the raw, granular data of contemporary digital life. By integrating these diverse methods, we gain a panoramic view of how digital activism functions both as a platform for discourse and as a tangible mechanism for legal and social change. We acknowledge the limitations of digital-only research, ensuring that our data is grounded in the lived realities of our participants, thereby validating digital findings through offline ethnographic cross-referencing.

3. Case Studies: The Digital Anatomy of Resistance

Case Study 1: The #DalitLivesMatter Campaign

This movement gained massive momentum in Mumbai, Delhi, and Bangalore, drawing critical parallels between global racial justice movements and Indian caste oppression. Unlike conventional protests, the campaign utilized "viral witnessing," where bystander videos of caste-based violence provided immediate, unfiltered evidence, forcing state accountability. The campaign forced mainstream media, often accused of ignoring caste atrocities, to engage with the reality of systematic violence, thus expanding the scope of the public conversation and creating a cross-generational dialogue about rights. By turning smartphones into tools of forensic accountability, the movement systematically dismantled the state’s monopoly on the "truth," compelling legal interventions where previously silence was the default. The campaign also served as a training ground for digital literacy, as activists developed sophisticated techniques to bypass content moderation filters that often disproportionately flag protest-related imagery.

Case Study 2: Digital Archiving Projects

Platforms such as "Dalit Camera" and various crowd-sourced archiving initiatives have pioneered the democratization of history. By capturing thousands of hours of oral histories from elderly community members, these projects create a non-institutional archive that challenges the sanitized, upper-caste historical narratives typically promoted by state hegemonies. This project of "counter-archiving" serves as a vital bulwark against historical erasure. It ensures that subaltern memory survives in the digital record, providing a repository for future generations to reclaim their heritage. This decentralization of the historical record is a profound rejection of the state's role as the sole arbiter of national memory. By transforming the "private" stories of discrimination into a "public" record, these archives force a re-evaluation of national milestones and symbols.

Case Study 3: Educational Advocacy Platforms

Digital mentorship networks serve as a critical, decentralized infrastructure for students entering higher education. By providing transparent, community-led resources on scholarships, entrance exam strategies, and networking, these platforms circumvent the informal, exclusive "caste-networks" (often referred to as 'merit' channels) that have historically barred Dalits from elite professional and academic spaces. This peer-to-peer knowledge sharing effectively levels the playing field, providing students with the "social capital" necessary to navigate institutional barriers that are often designed to exclude those without generational privilege. These networks demonstrate how digital community-building acts as a substitute for exclusionary kinship networks. As these networks scale, they have also begun to challenge the very definition of "merit," highlighting the structural barriers embedded in competitive exams.

Case Study 4: Urban Land Rights Activism

Using GIS-based digital mapping and community crowdsourcing, activists in peri-urban areas document state and private land encroachment. This "geo-resistance" allows communities to present localized, data-driven evidence in courts. By digitizing historical land deeds and overlaying them with real-time mapping technology, activists transform intangible, historical oral claims into actionable legal assets, effectively turning the digital map into a weapon of legal struggle. This application of technology bridges the gap between grassroots memory and formal legal requirements, transforming land struggles into technical, evidence-based disputes that are much harder for traditional power structures to dismiss. Through the synthesis of satellite imagery and community testimony, these projects expose the systematic displacement occurring under the guise of urban development.

5. Sociological Implications: Towards a New Theory of Agency

The findings suggest that digital resistance is not a peripheral activity but a central mechanism for contemporary Dalit assertion. By creating decentralized networks, activists are effectively "hacking" the social hierarchy. The digital space allows for a horizontal dissemination of information that bypasses the vertical power structures inherent in traditional caste society. However, this is tempered by the reality of digital surveillance and algorithmic bias, which continue to reflect the structural inequities of the physical world. The "digital divide" is not merely a lack of hardware; it is a manifestation of historical caste-based resource exclusion. As we transition into a digital-first governance model, the ability to command digital space becomes synonymous with the ability to participate in public life. Consequently, Neo-Dalit digital resistance serves as a corrective, an attempt to democratize a virtual landscape that threatens to replicate the exclusion of the physical one. This suggests a new theory of "networked agency" where the subaltern voice is not a singular cry but a distributed, persistent, and increasingly coordinated force that challenges the static, ritualized hierarchies of the past with a dynamic, fluid, and strategically mobilized present. The interplay of algorithmic capital and social identity suggests that the future of caste politics lies in the contestation of the digital architecture itself, requiring a deeper engagement with the politics of code, data ownership, and technological sovereignty.

Conclusion

Digital resistance represents a robust, multifaceted approach to challenging entrenched caste hegemony in urban India. By utilizing digital platforms, Neo-Dalit movements have successfully shifted the locus of political agency from traditional, rigid institutional structures to decentralized, networked spaces. This transformation has profound implications for urban democracy, suggesting that the "digital" is no longer a peripheral, passive space, but a core, active site where the future of caste, citizenship, and social justice is actively negotiated, contested, and ultimately redefined. The resilience shown by these movements suggests that even in a highly mediated world, the impulse toward equality remains the most potent, and now, the most viral, force in public life. The future of Dalit politics will increasingly rely on the navigation of these dual realities—the physical persistence of caste and the digital promise of liberation—ensuring that the struggle for annihilation of caste remains as current and vital as it has ever been. As technological integration deepens, the imperative for a nuanced, subaltern-informed digital policy becomes clear, framing the digital realm as a crucial, ongoing, and dynamic territory of liberation in the long, historic quest for dignity and equality.

metadata.title: Collaborative Tools and Communication Platforms for Remote Learning
metadata.description: The COVID-19 pandemic has dramatically transformed the educational landscape, rapidly accelerating the global shift toward remote learning and emphasizing the urgent need for robust and effective collaborative tools and communication platforms. As schools and universities adapted to the unprecedented circumstances of widespread lockdowns and physical distancing, these technologies became essential for maintaining instructional continuity and fostering student engagement in virtual environments. This review delves into the existing body of literature on the subject, critically analysing the effectiveness of various collaborative tools and communication platforms in supporting remote learning. It also explores the challenges that educators and institutions have faced in implementing these technologies, such as issues related to technical difficulties, equity, access, and the digital divide. Furthermore, the review outlines best practices for integrating these tools into educational frameworks, stressing the importance of adequate teacher training, inclusive access, and supportive learning environments to ensure the successful adoption and sustained use of these technologies. By offering a comprehensive understanding of these key areas, this study aims to provide valuable insights for educational institutions seeking to enhance their remote learning programmes and optimise student outcomes in a post-pandemic world.

metadata.title: AI Chatbots And Customer Loyalty: A Systematic Literature Review
metadata.description: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed customer service delivery across industries, with AI-powered chatbots emerging as pivotal tools for enhancing customer interactions and fostering loyalty. This systematic literature review synthesizes empirical evidence from peer-reviewed studies published between 2019 and 2026 to examine the relationship between AI chatbot service quality and customer loyalty. Following PRISMA guidelines, this review analyzes 62 articles sourced from Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore databases. The findings reveal that chatbot service quality dimensions—including response time, information quality, perceived usefulness, personalization, and anthropomorphic characteristics—significantly influence customer loyalty through the mediating mechanisms of customer satisfaction and trust. The Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and SERVQUAL emerge as the predominant theoretical frameworks underpinning this research domain. This review contributes to the academic discourse by providing an integrative conceptual framework, identifying research gaps, and offering strategic implications for organizations seeking to leverage AI chatbots for customer retention in the digital economy.
